June 10, 2026  
 
 
Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services  
7500 Security Blvd 
Baltimore, MD 21244  
 
RE: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; 
Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage 
Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children's Health 
Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualified 
Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges 
 
Submitted electronically via www.regulations.gov 
National Patient Advocate Foundation (NPAF) appreciates the opportunity to submit comments 
on this proposed rule.  
 
Background 
NPAF prioritizes policies responsive to unmet financial needs articulated by patients and 
caregivers coping with complex and chronic conditions. For most of them, financial distress is a 
common consequence of serious illness. This is true even for individuals with health insurance. 
Costs of medical and other care escalate quickly and often overwhelm even the best planned 
household budgets, hurting individuals' economies, health, and quality of life.  Patients and 
family caregivers in our vast national network consistently tell us that preserving financial 
stability alongside medical and mental health must be considered as integral aspects of high-
quality healthcare, and NPAF is positioned to pursue this objective through evidence-
supported, system-level reforms.  
 
Our direct patient services counterpart, Patient Advocate Foundation (PAF), delivers a hands-
on, skilled "Needs Navigation" model with and on behalf of patients experiencing financial 
hardship to help reduce the stress they and their caregivers experience in successfully 
completing the time-consuming administrative processes needed to access care and benefits. In 
2025, PAF reached more than 3.4 million people via direct services, education, and outreach, 
distributing over $259 million in financial support and providing direct, sustained assistance to 
more than 186,000 patients. The population PAF served last year alone represented 758

distinct diagnoses and 434 rare diseases from all 50 states, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the U.S. 
Virgin Islands, reaching patients in 92% of all U.S. counties. 
 
Needs navigation aims to ease healthcare cost concerns that are a common condition across 
patient populations.  NPAF worked with patients and caregivers to define and describe the 
need for it in terms that are resonant and responsive to their challenges as they've identified 
them:  
 
Provided hands-on by individuals skilled in communication and resource coordination, 
Needs Navigation helps secure access to safety net services and other responsive 
assistance personalized to preserve patient and family financial health.   
 
NPAF recognizes the importance of making Needs Navigation models reliably available to help 
people with cost concerns in every care setting – hospitals, outpatient offices, skilled nursing 
facilities, community health centers and more.  This is one of our top policy priorities for 
improving quality in the context of advancing person-centered, value-based care.  A variety of 
clinical and non-clinical navigation models have evolved over the past decades in different care 
settings as a critical component of providing person-centered care, including Needs Navigation 
to help patients and families make ends meet and maintain their financial health while 
contending with their complex and chronic conditions.  
 
Evidence indicates the striking necessity of expanding the availability of Needs Navigation 
models now, with a 2024 Gallup poll showing more than one-third of Americans (35%) 
reporting that they are unable to access quality, affordable healthcare – findings that are four 
points higher than in 2023 and a new high since 2021. A 2025 national survey of 2,510 patients 
and caregivers fielded by our PAF Patient Insight Institute found 82% of them experienced 
financial difficulties in the past year because of expenditures related to medical care, insurance, 
cost of living challenges, lost wages, and more.  The majority of this cohort also confirmed that 
Needs Navigation should be available for everyone (89%), with 95% responding that they 
valued Needs Navigation as a vital part of healthcare.  
 
Recognizing the rising prevalence of financial hardship across patient populations, Needs 
Navigation should now be expanded and integrated as a care model across all Medicare 
programs to provide real-time relief and practical help for patients and families at risk for 
medical debt, other health-related financial hardships, and social strains that contribute to 
poorer health outcomes.   
 
With this background, here are our comments on this proposed rule:

Decision timeframes for drug PA
NPAF supports the proposal to establish shorter and more aligned decision timeframes for prior 
authorization (PA) of drugs across Medicare Advantage (MA), Medicaid, CHIP, and Qualified 
Health Plans. For patients living with financial hardship, even brief delays in medication access 
can trigger missed work, worsening health, avoidable emergency care, and out-of-pocket 
spending they cannot absorb; faster decisions are therefore not only an access protection but a 
financial protection.

NPAF particularly supports cross-program alignment because fragmented timelines shift the 
burden of navigating coverage rules onto patients and families with the fewest resources, least 
schedule flexibility, and least ability to pay cash while waiting. A more predictable timeline 
across programs will reduce treatment disruptions and help protect lower-income patients from 
the cascading financial harms that follow a preventable gap in medication access. Needs 
navigation services would also be helpful for patients to navigate through these often complex 
systems.  
PA Application Programming Interfaces (API) for drugs
NPAF supports the proposed sections extending the PA API and related interoperability 
requirements to drugs. Patients should not learn that a medication is effectively inaccessible 
only after arriving at the pharmacy, especially when they do not have the savings, credit, 
transportation flexibility, or paid leave needed to absorb repeated delays and coverage 
surprises.

Standardized, electronic PA can reduce avoidable administrative friction that falls hardest on 
people with low incomes and on the community clinicians who serve them. When coverage 
requirements are visible and actionable earlier in the prescribing process, patients are less likely 
to face unaffordable cash prices, repeated co-pays tied to failed utilization-management steps, 
or treatment abandonment caused by opaque plan processes. Again, adding Needs Navigation 
would help ensure patients get the care they need.
Specific denial reasons and detailed PA data in access APIs
NPAF supports the proposal requiring specific reasons for drug PA denials and requiring detailed 
PA data to be available through patient, provider, and payer-to-payer interoperability pathways. 
Patients experiencing financial hardship are harmed not only by denials themselves, but also by 
vague or generic denial notices that make it impossible to correct an error quickly or pursue an 
effective appeal before a condition worsens.

Clear denial rationales and accessible authorization data can shorten delays, reduce needless 
repeat submissions, and help patients, caregivers, navigators, and providers document the real-
world consequences of utilization management. These transparency protections are especially 
important for low-income patients, who are more likely to forgo treatment, incur debt, or 
switch to a less appropriate therapy when coverage obstacles are confusing and time-
consuming to contest.
API usage metrics and reporting to CMS
NPAF supports the proposal requiring impacted payers to report API endpoints and annual API 
usage metrics to CMS. Accountability is essential, because interoperability requirements will not 
meaningfully protect patients if plans can appear compliant on paper while maintaining 
workflows that continue to delay treatment and shift hidden costs onto patients.

These reporting sections create the foundation for oversight of whether electronic PA tools are 
actually being used in ways that improve access for patients with limited financial means. Strong 
reporting can help CMS and external stakeholders identify plans whose utilization-management 
practices continue to impose disproportionate burdens on people enrolled in Medicaid, CHIP, 
MA, and Marketplace coverage.
Scope of impacted payers
NPAF supports the proposal to apply these protections across the full range of impacted payers, 
including MA organizations, Medicaid and CHIP fee-for-service and managed care programs, and 
Qualified Health Plan issuers on the federally facilitated Exchanges, including FF-SHOP where 
applicable. Financial hardship is not confined to one coverage source, and patients should not 
lose basic transparency and timeliness protections merely because their income, employment, 
or eligibility category changes.

Instability in income and coverage is itself a driver of financial hardship, and coverage 
transitions are precisely the moments when patients are most vulnerable to medication 
interruptions and unexpected costs. (For that reason, we are very concerned about the upcoming 
Medicaid spending cuts, new work requirements, and the stringent eligibility criteria proposed for 
people coping with complex, chronic and disabling conditions.) Cross-program consistency is 
therefore necessary to protect continuity of treatment and to reduce the financial harm 
associated with churn between Medicaid, CHIP, MA, and Marketplace coverage.
HIPAA administrative simplification and FHIR standards for PA transactions
NPAF supports adopting standardized FHIR-based approaches for PA-related transactions under 
HIPAA administrative simplification. Administrative complexity is not a neutral systems issue; for 
patients with financial hardship, it often translates directly into delayed care, extra 
appointments, unpaid time away from work, transportation expenses, and worsening illness 
that becomes more expensive to treat.

Also, under-resourced providers and safety-net settings should not be forced to navigate 
fragmented, proprietary workflows that undermine timely access to medications for low-
income patients. Greater standardization can reduce inequities in who benefits from 
interoperability and helps ensure that patients served in Medicaid-heavy, rural, and community-
based settings are not left behind.
Requests for Information
- Step therapy (RFI)- We appreciate the opportunity to provide input on how technology 
and data sharing (especially the Payer-to-Payer API) could be used so payers honor prior 
step-therapy determinations when a patient switches plans.
- API quality- We feel that API testing/certification should explicitly assess whether 
patients actually experience fewer cash-pay episodes, abandoned prescriptions, or 
debt-generating care as a result of improved electronic PA.
analysis:
## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** National Patient Advocate Foundation (NPAF), submitted by Rebecca A. Kirch, Executive Vice President, Policy and Programs
- **Stakeholder type:** Advocacy Group
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** 30 years of organizational experience in patient advocacy; sister organization Patient Advocate Foundation (PAF) served 3.4 million people in 2025, distributed $259 million in financial support, directly assisted 186,000+ patients across 758 diagnoses and 434 rare diseases in 92% of U.S. counties.

---

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

NPAF broadly supports the proposed rule's drug PA provisions, framing all major components through the lens of financial hardship for patients with complex and chronic conditions. The organization supports shorter PA decision timeframes, PA APIs for drugs, specific denial reasons, API usage metrics, broad payer scope, and FHIR-based HIPAA standardization. NPAF recommends that step therapy history be transferred across payers and that API certification include outcome-based patient financial health metrics.

---

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS, PA-DRUG-MEDICAL, PA-DRUG-PHARMACY, PA-DENIAL-REASONS, API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING, API-USAGE-METRICS, FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS, HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** None cited explicitly
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR (generally), Payer-to-Payer API

---

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Drug PA Decision Timeframes**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Delays cause missed work, worsening health, avoidable ER visits, and unaffordable out-of-pocket costs for low-income patients. Cross-program alignment removes the burden of navigating fragmented timelines from the least-resourced patients.
- **Specific request:** Finalize the proposed timeframes; integrate Needs Navigation services to help patients navigate the system.

**Topic 2: PA API for Drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL, PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Patients—especially those with low incomes—should not learn of medication inaccessibility at the pharmacy; electronic PA reduces administrative friction that disproportionately harms low-income patients and their clinicians.
- **Specific request:** Finalize PA API extension; integrate Needs Navigation alongside electronic PA tools.

**Topic 3: Specific Denial Reasons**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Vague denials prevent timely error correction and effective appeals, causing low-income patients to forgo treatment, incur debt, or switch to less appropriate therapies.
- **Specific request:** Finalize requirement for specific, actionable denial rationales accessible through all interoperability APIs.

**Topic 4: API Endpoint Reporting and Usage Metrics**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING, API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Accountability is essential; plans could appear compliant while maintaining workflows that delay treatment and shift hidden costs to patients. Reporting enables identification of plans imposing disproportionate burdens.
- **Specific request:** Maintain robust reporting requirements to enable external oversight.

**Topic 5: Scope of Impacted Payers (including FF-SHOP)**
- **Provision ID:** FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Financial hardship is not confined to one coverage type; patients should not lose protections due to income or eligibility changes. Coverage transitions are peak moments of vulnerability.
- **Specific request:** Maintain broad payer scope; expressed concern about Medicaid spending cuts and new work requirements harming transition-period patients.

**Topic 6: FHIR as HIPAA Standard for PA Transactions**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Administrative complexity translates to delayed care, extra appointments, lost wages, and worsening illness for financially vulnerable patients. Standardization helps safety-net and rural providers serve low-income patients equitably.
- **Specific request:** Finalize FHIR-based standardization; ensure under-resourced providers are not left behind.

---

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S20:** NPAF supports the proposed 24-hour expedited and standard drug PA timeframes, emphasizing the financial protection value of faster decisions for low-income patients.
- **S43:** Supports cross-program alignment of PA timeframes, noting that fragmented timelines burden patients with the fewest resources.
- **S12/S15:** Supports extending PA API to medical and pharmacy benefit drugs, noting that early coverage visibility reduces cash-pay episodes and treatment abandonment.
- **S16:** Supports requiring specific denial reasons, emphasizing that vague notices disproportionately harm low-income patients unable to navigate complex appeals.
- **S23/S24:** Supports API endpoint reporting as an accountability mechanism.
- **S29/S30/S34/S35:** Supports API usage metrics collection and reporting; recommends metrics include patient-level financial outcome indicators.
- **S40/S41/S42:** Supports extending requirements to FF-SHOP; cross-program consistency protects patients during coverage transitions.
- **S44/S45:** Supports FHIR as HIPAA standard for PA transactions, arguing standardization reduces inequities in interoperability benefits.
- **S54:** Recommends API testing/certification explicitly assess whether patients experience fewer cash-pay episodes, abandoned prescriptions, or debt-generating care (S54, quality/certification dimension).
- **S66-S82 (Step therapy RFI):** Recommends CMS require plans to honor completed step-therapy steps across payers via Payer-to-Payer API, and track cumulative out-of-pocket costs associated with step-therapy sequences, with special attention to Medicaid, CHIP, and low-income MA/QHP populations.

---

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize shorter, cross-program aligned drug PA decision timeframes.
2. Finalize extension of PA API and interoperability requirements to drugs (medical and pharmacy benefit).
3. Finalize requirement for specific, actionable denial reasons accessible through all interoperability pathways.
4. Maintain robust API endpoint and usage metrics reporting to enable external accountability.
5. Apply interoperability protections across all impacted payer types, including FF-SHOP.
6. Finalize FHIR-based HIPAA standardization for PA transactions.
7. Require plans to honor completed step-therapy steps when patients switch payers (using Payer-to-Payer API).
8. Track cumulative out-of-pocket costs and delays associated with step-therapy sequences, especially for Medicaid, CHIP, and low-income MA/QHP populations.
9. Require API testing/certification to assess patient-level financial outcomes (fewer cash-pay episodes, abandoned prescriptions, debt-generating care).
10. Integrate Needs Navigation models across Medicare programs to address financial hardship in real time.

---

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Financial hardship cascades from PA delays; opaque denial processes; fragmented timelines disproportionately harming low-income patients; upcoming Medicaid spending cuts and work requirements threaten coverage continuity.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Treatment abandonment, medical debt, avoidable emergency care, worsening illness, lost wages when PA delays occur.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Under-resourced providers and safety-net settings struggling with fragmented, proprietary workflows; risk that plans pass technical compliance while patients still face hardship.

---

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** 2024 Gallup poll: 35% of Americans unable to access quality, affordable healthcare (4 points higher than 2023). 2025 PAF Patient Insight Institute survey (n=2,510): 82% experienced financial difficulties from medical care costs; 89% said Needs Navigation should be available for everyone; 95% valued it as vital. PAF 2025: reached 3.4 million people, distributed $259 million, directly assisted 186,000+ patients across 758 diagnoses, 434 rare diseases, 92% of U.S. counties.
- **Studies or research referenced:** PAF Patient Insight Institute national survey (2025); Gallup poll (2024).
- **Examples provided:** Patients arriving at pharmacy to find medication inaccessible; patients unable to afford cash prices while awaiting PA resolution.

---

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Low-income patients and caregivers; Medicaid, CHIP, MA, and QHP enrollees; safety-net providers; community clinicians; Needs Navigation professionals.
- **Economic implications:** Faster PA and clearer denials reduce medical debt, avoidable ER use, treatment abandonment, and cascading financial harm for low-income populations.
- **Technical feasibility:** Not directly assessed; supports proposed measures with emphasis on equity in implementation.
- **Patient care impact:** Significant—delays in drug PA cause missed work, worsening health, avoidable emergency care, and financial destabilization.

---

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive
- **Tone:** Collaborative, patient-centered, advocacy-focused
- **Priority level:** High

---

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "For patients living with financial hardship, even brief delays in medication access can trigger missed work, worsening health, avoidable emergency care, and out-of-pocket spending they cannot absorb; faster decisions are therefore not only an access protection but a financial protection." - Context: Supporting shorter drug PA decision timeframes.

2. "Patients should not learn that a medication is effectively inaccessible only after arriving at the pharmacy, especially when they do not have the savings, credit, transportation flexibility, or paid leave needed to absorb repeated delays and coverage surprises." - Context: Supporting PA API extension to drugs.

3. "Accountability is essential, because interoperability requirements will not meaningfully protect patients if plans can appear compliant on paper while maintaining workflows that continue to delay treatment and shift hidden costs onto patients." - Context: Supporting API endpoint and usage metrics reporting.

4. "Administrative complexity is not a neutral systems issue; for patients with financial hardship, it often translates directly into delayed care, extra appointments, unpaid time away from work, transportation expenses, and worsening illness that becomes more expensive to treat." - Context: Supporting FHIR as HIPAA standard for PA transactions.

---

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Supports cross-program alignment of PA decision timeframes to protect patients during coverage transitions.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - Primary frame: financial hardship cascades from PA delays; lower-income patients cannot absorb cash costs during delays.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - Central theme throughout; all provisions analyzed through equity lens for low-income, Medicaid-heavy, rural, and community-based populations.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - PA delays causing treatment abandonment, prescription abandonment, and avoidable ER use for financially vulnerable patients.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Supports specific denial reasons and PA data in APIs as essential transparency protections for low-income patients.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Criticizes fragmented, proprietary workflows that disadvantage under-resourced safety-net providers and their patients.
- [x] **HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS** (as EXISTING-WORKFLOWS corollary) - Supports FHIR standardization to reduce inequities in who benefits from interoperability.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Recommends step-therapy data transfer via Payer-to-Payer API across coverage transitions.
- [x] **SMALL-PAYER-IMPACT** - Indirectly: concern that under-resourced providers (not plans) may struggle with fragmented workflows; supports FF-SHOP inclusion.
